newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIAN PRESIDENT TO START TALKS ON NEW CABINET.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIAN PRESIDENT TO START TALKS ON NEW CABINET.

text.p: Bulgarian President Zhelyu Zhelev will start consultations on Monday on formation of a new government following the resignation of Prime Minister Zhan Videnov.

In a speech to the nation on Sunday, Zhelev said the shortcomings of Videnov's government had been obvious a year ago and he regretted that as president of a parliamentary republic he lacked the power to dismiss the cabinet himself.

"If Bulgaria was a presidential republic where the president had the right to appoint and dismiss the prime minister, I would have dismissed Mr Videnov and his government long ago in order to promote more responsible and competent people," Zhelev said.
"The current severe economic crisis could have been avoided and our country could have developed in a totally different way."
Videnov tendered his resignation at a congress of his ruling Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) on December 21 and it was accepted by parliament on Saturday.
Increasingly under fire for his handling of the economy, he said he felt he lacked the support he needed to continue as prime minister and party leader.
The Socialists are the biggest party in parliament and Zhelev must first ask them to form a government.
According to the constitution, they then have a week in which to do so.

"Even now the BSP has the possibility to rule the country until the end of its mandate with little respect for where Bulgaria is going. This is possible even after the failure of Videnov, which is not only a failure of his government, but of the whole policy of the BSP," Zhelev said.
The ex-communist government's failure to carry out prescribed economic reforms has led to suspension of funding from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank.
Fourteen illiquid banks have been placed in receivership and the lev has fallen from 70 at the beginning of 1996 to about 500 now.
Economists say the social and economic cost of reforms will be far greater now than if they had been carried out sooner.

A new prime minister must negotiate with the IMF on the planned introduction of a currency board fixed exchange rate regime to stabilise the lev, and withstand criticism of the intitial hardship exected to accompany its implementation.

Possible premiers include the speaker of parliament Blagovest Sendov, Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, and U.S.-born former foreign minister Georgi Pirinski, who resigned last month after a party confidence vote gave Videnov only narrow backing.
Zhelev is due to leave office next month and hand over to opposition lawyer Petar Stoyanov, who was elected in November.
